items.title: Your body can make antibodies against molecules that don't exist yet
items.claim: Humans have about 20,000 genes. We make perhaps 10 to the 11 different antibody molecules — far more than our genome could encode directly. Including antibodies against viruses we'll never meet.
items.prompt: How do we generate such enormous antibody diversity?

options.text: Each antibody is encoded by a separate gene

V(D)J recombination — during B cell development, gene segments (V, D, J) are randomly chosen and joined with imprecise cuts, and then somatic hypermutation refines the result during an immune response
Antibodies are made up new for each encounter from scratch
The genome reshuffles itself constantly in all cells

items.reveal_title: Tonegawa's discovery — recombination in somatic cells
items.reveal:
Susumu Tonegawa (Nobel 1987) showed that B cells deliberately rearrange their immunoglobulin genes. Each B cell randomly picks one V, one D and one J segment for the heavy chain (V and J for the light chain), joins them with imprecise junctions (adding/deleting nucleotides), and pairs heavy with light. The combinatorial maths gives about 10 to the 11 possible specificities from a few hundred gene segments.

Once a B cell encounters its antigen, somatic hypermutation introduces additional point mutations into the variable region, and selection retains the best binders (affinity maturation).

The result is an immune system that can respond to virtually any molecular shape — including ones never seen before, like artificial drugs.
items.why: Genome size limits direct encoding. The immune system uses combinatorics and somatic mutation to overshoot what the genome alone could specify.

items.title: A tumour is a tiny evolving ecosystem
items.claim: Cancer cells accumulate mutations. Cells with mutations that confer growth advantages dominate. Drug treatment kills the susceptible cells but spares resistant ones — which then dominate the regrown tumour.
items.prompt: Why is cancer so hard to cure even with effective drugs?

options.text: Drugs don't work on cancer cells

A tumour contains millions to billions of slightly genetically different cells; selection pressure from a drug acts on the existing variation and rapidly enriches resistant clones — the same evolutionary process as antibiotic resistance, but inside a single patient

items.reveal_title: Tumour heterogeneity and the cost of monotherapy
items.reveal:
Single-cell sequencing of tumours reveals enormous clonal diversity. A 5 cm tumour may contain 10 to the 9 cells, each with its own profile of acquired mutations. Subclones can have different drug sensitivities, growth rates and metastatic potentials.

Treating with a single targeted therapy selects for whichever cells are pre-existingly resistant. Within months, the tumour regrows — now dominated by the resistant subclone. Combination therapy (targeting multiple pathways at once) makes resistance much less likely, by analogy with HIV's HAART protocol.

The Peter Nowell paper (1976) first proposed clonal evolution in cancer. Recent decades have made it the dominant framework, with implications for drug strategy, biomarker design, and the inevitability of resistance.
items.why: Cancer is taught as one disease. It's an evolving population of cells subject to selection — making it as much an ecological and evolutionary problem as a medical one.

items.title: Stomata are tiny mouths that decide between starving and drying
items.claim: A leaf has hundreds of stomata per square millimetre. Open them: CO2 enters for photosynthesis but water evaporates away. Close them: water is saved but photosynthesis stalls. Plants must decide minute by minute.
items.prompt: How do guard cells open and close the stomatal pore?

options.text: Guard cells actively pump K+ ions in; water follows by osmosis; the cell swells; thicker inner walls force the cell to bow outward, opening the pore. Reverse the process to close

items.reveal:
Each stoma is bordered by two guard cells. Their inner walls (facing the pore) are thicker and less elastic than their outer walls.

Opening: blue light activates a proton pump (H+-ATPase). The cells become more negative inside; K+ flows in via channels. Cl- and malate follow. Water enters by osmosis. Turgor rises. The thinner outer walls expand more than the inner walls, pulling the cells apart and opening the pore.

Closing: ABA (abscisic acid, the drought-stress hormone) triggers K+ efflux. The cells lose water and shrink. The pore closes.

Most plants close stomata at night (no photosynthesis needed) and during drought. CAM plants invert this. Wheat loses ~500 kg of water per kg of grain produced — most through stomata.

Climate change is forcing plants to evolve stomatal density: rising CO2 lets leaves get the same carbon with fewer stomata, reducing water loss.
items.why: Stomatal regulation is the central trade-off of land plant life. Engineering stomata for higher water-use efficiency is a major target of crop science.
